problem: Every organization holds data that not everyone should be able to touch: payroll files, customer KYC documents, ethics case emails, source code, HR records. Without a reliable permission system, a business has exactly two bad options — lock everything down so tightly that people can't do their jobs, or leave things open enough that anyone with access to a machine can read, alter, or delete anything.

Permissions are the mechanism that lets an organization say precisely who can read a file, who can change it, who can run it as a program, and who can delete it — without needing a human to manually watch every access. Get this wrong and the business faces very real consequences:
A support agent with unnecessary write access to a shared configuration file accidentally (or maliciously) breaks a production script everyone depends on.
A departing employee's account retains access to sensitive folders because permissions were tied to the individual rather than a managed group.
A compromised low-privilege account becomes a company-wide ransomware incident because "Everyone: Full Control" was applied for convenience.
An auditor asks "who can access customer financial data" and no one can answer quickly, because permissions were never documented or centrally managed.
A junior developer's script runs with root/Administrator rights it never needed, turning a small bug into a system-wide outage.

Permissions are the enforcement arm of the security principle of least privilege — the technical mechanism that turns a policy decision ("only Finance should see payroll") into something the operating system actually honors on every single access attempt.
concept: A permission is a rule, attached to a file, folder, or system resource, that defines which identities (users, groups, processes) may perform which actions (read, write, execute, delete, modify) on that resource.
Permissions are enforced by the operating system kernel itself, at the moment of access — not by convention, not by hiding things, but by an actual gatekeeping check every single time.
Two core models dominate enterprise IT, and understanding both — and how they differ — is the heart of this session:
POSIX permissions (Linux/Unix/macOS) — a simple, fixed model: every file has one owner, one group, and a set of "other" rules, each expressed as read/write/execute bits.

ACL-based permissions (Windows NTFS, and POSIX ACL extensions on Linux) — a flexible model where any number of individual users or groups can each be granted or denied specific rights on the same object.

A simple mental model: POSIX permissions are like a house with three keys — one for the owner, one for the family (group), and one spare for everyone else. NTFS ACLs are like a hotel keycard system where the front desk can grant or revoke access to any specific room for any specific guest, independently, at any time.
deep: 3.1 POSIX permissions (Linux/Unix) Every file has three permission classes — owner (u), group (g), and others (o) — and three basic rights per class: read (r), write (w), execute (x). These are stored as bits in the file's inode metadata and are commonly displayed as a 10-character string, e.g. -rwxr-xr--.

Field Meaning Position 1 File type: - (regular file), d (directory), l (symlink) Positions 2–4 Owner permissions (rwx) Positions 5–7 Group permissions (rwx) Positions 8–10 Other/world permissions (rwx) Numeric (octal) notation assigns read=4, write=2, execute=1 per class, summed together — chmod 750 means owner=7 (rwx), group=5 (r-x), other=0 (none). This is the notation used constantly in scripts and automation.

SUID (Set User ID, 4000) — when set on an executable, it runs with the file owner's privileges rather than the invoking user's (classic example: /usr/bin/passwd runs as root so any user can update the shared password file).
SGID (Set Group ID, 2000) — similar, but for group identity; on a directory, it makes new files inherit the directory's group automatically, which is heavily used for shared team folders.
Sticky bit (1000) — on a directory (e.g., /tmp), it restricts deletion so only a file's owner (or root) can remove it, even if others have write access to the directory.

3.3 POSIX ACLs (extended) Because classic POSIX only supports one owner and one group, Linux added ACL extensions (getfacl / setfacl) to allow multiple named users or groups to have distinct permissions on a single file — closing the gap with Windows-style ACLs while remaining backward compatible.

3.4 Windows NTFS ACLs NTFS permissions are stored as a Discretionary Access Control List (DACL) attached to each file/folder's security descriptor. The DACL is an ordered list of Access Control Entries (ACEs), each naming a security principal (user or group SID) and either Allow or Deny for specific rights (Full Control, Modify, Read & Execute, List Folder Contents, Read, Write, and granular advanced permissions beneath those).

Evaluation order matters: Windows evaluates explicit Deny entries before explicit Allow entries, and explicit permissions before inherited ones — an explicit Deny anywhere in the chain wins, regardless of how many Allows exist elsewhere.

Inheritance: permissions set on a parent folder propagate down to child objects by default; this is efficient but is also the most common source of over-broad, hard-to-audit access if not managed carefully.

Effective Access: the actual resulting permission for a user is the combination of their own explicit/inherited ACEs plus every group they belong to — this is why "why can't they access X" troubleshooting always requires checking group membership, not just the file's ACL.
workflow: In daily operations, permissions work shows up as a constant, recurring set of tasks:
Provisioning access: when a new hire joins, adding their account to the correct security groups (Session 22 — Groups) rather than granting permissions to the individual directly.
Access requests: handling "I need access to X folder/share" tickets — the correct workflow checks against a role-based access model rather than granting ad hoc permissions.
Offboarding: removing group memberships (or disabling the account entirely) the moment someone leaves, so access is revoked instantly rather than lingering.
Periodic access review / recertification: audits where folder owners confirm that everyone with access still needs it — a standard compliance requirement (SOX, ISO 27001, PCI-DSS).
Troubleshooting Access Denied tickets: the single most common permissions-related support ticket, requiring a methodical check of explicit ACEs, inherited ACEs, and group membership.

Scripted enforcement: using chmod/chown/setfacl in Linux configuration management, or PowerShell (Get-Acl/Set-Acl, icacls) in Windows automation, to keep permissions consistent and self-healing rather than manually set once and forgotten.
enterprise: Permissions sit at the intersection of three layers in this roadmap: they are stored as File System metadata (Layer 2, the previous session), they are assigned to Users and Groups (Layer 2, sessions 21-22), and they are one of the foundational controls of the entire Security layer (Layer 6) — specifically the Least Privilege and AAA (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting) principles covered later.

In a Windows enterprise: Active Directory security groups (Layer 4) are mapped onto NTFS folder ACLs (Layer 2), and Group Policy can further restrict what's possible even for an authorized user. In Linux:

users and groups (Layer 2) map onto file ownership and POSIX/ACL permissions directly, often layered with SELinux or AppArmor mandatory access control for an additional, non-discretionary layer the file owner can't override.
This is a layer that never operates alone — permissions without correctly structured groups (Session 22) become unmanageable, and groups without correctly applied permissions accomplish nothing.

6. Dependencies (what Permissions rely on) Depends On Why File Systems (Session 19) Permissions are literally stored as metadata inside the file system (inode mode bits, NTFS security descriptors) — there is no permission without a file system to hold it.
Kernel (Session 12) The kernel is the actual enforcement point; it checks permissions on every single system call that touches a file, before any user-space code runs.
Users (Session 21) Every permission ultimately resolves to a user identity (UID/SID) — permissions are meaningless without an identity system to check against.
Groups (Session 22) Enterprise-scale permission management is only maintainable when permissions are assigned to groups rather than hundreds of individuals.
Processes (Session 13) A running process inherits the permissions of the user account that launched it (or an escalated identity via SUID/sudo), which is what the kernel actually checks against.

7. Dependents (what relies on Permissions) Depends on Permissions Why Services (Session 17) Background services run under dedicated service accounts whose permissions determine exactly what that service can and cannot touch on the system.
Package Management (Session 23) Installing software system-wide requires elevated permissions — the entire model of "admin install" vs. "user install" is a permissions decision.
Active Directory / Group Policy (Sessions 52, 60) GPOs distribute and enforce NTFS/registry permissions at scale across thousands of machines.
Least Privilege / Zero Trust (Sessions 85, 87) These security principles are only real when permission systems actually enforce a minimal, verified set of rights per identity.
Incident Response / Forensics (Sessions 100-101) Investigating a breach always includes reconstructing exactly what permissions the compromised account had, to understand blast radius.
Backup (Session 78) Backup agents need carefully scoped elevated permissions to read all files for backup, which is itself a significant security design decision.
security: Least privilege: every account, service, and process should hold only the permissions it needs for its specific task — no more. This is the single most important operating principle for this entire topic.

Privilege escalation: attackers routinely exploit permission misconfigurations (a world-writable script run by root, a SUID binary with a bug, an overly generous sudoers entry) to jump from a low- privilege foothold to full system control.

Deny-overrides-Allow: understanding NTFS's evaluation order is a security-critical detail — a single misplaced explicit Deny or Allow ACE can either lock out a legitimate user or, more dangerously, silently grant access nobody intended.

Group nesting risk: adding a group to another group (nested groups) can silently grant far broader access than intended if the resulting effective permissions aren't reviewed — a very common audit finding.
SUID/SGID auditing: security teams routinely scan systems for unexpected SUID binaries (find / - perm -4000), since a rogue SUID root binary is a direct root-access backdoor.

Mandatory Access Control (MAC): SELinux and AppArmor add a layer that even the file owner cannot override — the file's discretionary ACL might allow an action, but a MAC policy can still block it, protecting against misconfigured or compromised owner accounts.
Ransomware blast radius: as in the Session 19 example, broad discretionary permissions (Everyone:
Full Control) are consistently one of the top root causes of large-scale ransomware damage, because malware simply inherits whatever access the compromised user already had.
troubleshooting: Symptom Likely Cause First Diagnostic Step "Access Denied" despite user being in the right AD group Explicit Deny ACE elsewhere in the chain, or stale Kerberos ticket / group membership not yet refreshed Check Effective Access tab in Windows; have user run klist purge or log off/on to refresh group tokens Linux "Permission denied" despite correct rwx bits SELinux/AppArmor MAC policy blocking the action independently of DAC permissions Check ausearch -m avc or /var/log/audit/audit.log; try setenforce 0 temporarily on a test box only chmod change doesn't seem to take effect ACL entries (setfacl) override base permission bits and weren't cleared Run getfacl on the file to check for extended ACL entries beyond the standard rwx New files in a shared folder have wrong group ownership SGID bit missing on the parent directory Check directory permissions for the 's' in the group execute position; set with chmod g+s Script fails only when run via cron / as a service, not interactively The service account has different (usually fewer) permissions than the interactive user Check which account the scheduled task/cron/service actually runs as, not the account that created it User can see a folder exists but not its contents List Folder Contents / Traverse permission present without Read permission on the underlying files Review granular NTFS advanced permissions, not just the basic Read/Modify/Full Control summary
example: A support/CEx organization (comparable to a FundedNext-style operations environment) manages daily case exports, KYC documents, and internal ethics-review emails on a shared drive. Early on, a well- meaning admin grants the entire support team's AD security group Modify access at the top-level share, reasoning it's simpler than managing permissions per subfolder.

Months later, an internal review finds that every support agent — regardless of tenure, role, or need — can read the Ethics Case folder, which contains sensitive internal investigation emails about specific employees, including some agents' own teammates. This isn't a hack or a breach; it's a permissions design flaw that was completely invisible day-to-day because nothing broke — the data was simply overexposed the entire time.

The fix follows the same pattern security teams apply broadly: subfolders are separated by sensitivity, dedicated AD groups are created per function (Support-Agents, Support-Leads, Ethics-Reviewers), NTFS ACLs are reapplied at the correct folder level instead of the top-level share, inheritance is broken where necessary, and a quarterly access review is scheduled. The technical change is straightforward NTFS ACL work — the harder part is realizing that convenient, broad permissions are a standing liability even when nothing has visibly gone wrong yet.
cloud: Cloud IAM (Session 123) generalizes the same concept beyond files: instead of "who can read this file," it's "who can invoke this API action on this resource," expressed as policy documents (AWS IAM policies, Azure RBAC roles, GCP IAM bindings) rather than file ACLs.

Cloud storage permissions still echo the file-system model: S3 bucket policies and ACLs, Azure Blob RBAC/SAS tokens, and Google Cloud Storage IAM all express read/write/delete rights on objects, just expressed as JSON policy rather than rwx bits.

A recurring real-world cloud incident pattern is the direct cloud equivalent of the "Everyone: Full Control" mistake — publicly readable S3 buckets or overly permissive IAM wildcard policies (Action: "*", Resource: "*") causing large-scale data exposure.

Cloud file services (Azure Files, AWS EFS/FSx) layer standard NTFS or POSIX permissions on top of the cloud IAM layer — so cloud file access can require satisfying both the identity platform's authorization AND the traditional file-level permission, in that order.
automation: Configuration management tools (Ansible, Puppet, Chef — Session 110) declaratively enforce permissions as code: an Ansible file module with mode: '0750' and owner/group fields ensures drift is corrected automatically rather than relying on someone remembering to run chmod.
PowerShell (Get-Acl, Set-Acl, icacls, NTFSSecurity module) is the standard way Windows admins script and audit NTFS permissions at scale across hundreds of servers.
Access review automation: scripts that periodically export "who has access to what" (e.g., dumping AD group membership joined against folder ACLs) turn a painful manual audit into a scheduled report.

CI/CD pipelines (Session 111) must carefully scope the permissions of their service accounts/deployment keys — a compromised pipeline with excessive permissions is a well-known modern supply-chain attack vector.

Infrastructure as Code (Terraform, ARM/Bicep, CloudFormation — Session 109) defines cloud IAM policies and NTFS/POSIX permissions on provisioned resources as version-controlled, reviewable code rather than manual console clicks.
career: Permissions work is one of the most consistently in-demand, hands-on skills across every IT career stage — precisely because "someone can't access something" or "someone can access something they shouldn't" never stops being a live business problem.

Help Desk / Support: the single most common ticket category ("I can't open this file/folder") requires fast, correct permissions diagnosis — exactly the terrain a CEx/support role like this one already lives in daily.
Sysadmin: designing group and folder structures that scale cleanly as an organization grows, without turning into unmanageable permission sprawl.
Security Analyst / Auditor: access reviews, least-privilege enforcement, and permission-based attack surface analysis are core, recurring responsibilities.
Cloud Engineer: IAM policy design is arguably the single most safety-critical skill in cloud infrastructure work — a single overly broad policy can expose an entire environment.
DevOps/Automation Engineer: writing the configuration-as-code that keeps permissions consistent and auditable across fleets of servers and cloud resources.

misconceptions: "If I can't see the file, no one can access it." — Hiding a file from a directory listing is not a permission control; the underlying access rights are what actually matter, and a hidden file with weak permissions is still fully exposed.
"Owner of a file can always do anything to it." — Under Mandatory Access Control (SELinux/AppArmor) or with an explicit Deny ACE, even the owner can be blocked from an action;
ownership is not an override of every other control.

"Removing someone from a group revokes their access immediately everywhere." — Access tokens (Kerberos tickets, cached credentials) can persist until refreshed; a user may retain old access for a period after group removal until they reauthenticate.
"Read access is harmless." — Read access to the wrong data (KYC documents, HR records, credentials in config files) can itself be the entire security incident; read is not automatically "safe."

"chmod 777 is a quick, harmless fix." — Granting full read/write/execute to everyone is almost never the correct fix and is one of the most common self-inflicted security holes in Linux environments, usually applied to make an error message go away without understanding the root cause.

"NTFS permissions and share permissions are the same thing." — Windows file shares actually apply two separate permission layers (share-level and NTFS-level); the effective access is the more restrictive of the two, which frequently surprises people troubleshooting access issues.
anchors: POSIX rwx = three keyrings on one keychain: owner, group, everyone else — always in that fixed order, always only those three.
chmod numbers = read(4) + write(2) + execute(1), like a simple point system per class — 7 means you unlocked all three, 5 means you skipped write.
NTFS Deny beats Allow = a bouncer's "no" always overrules a promoter's "yes," no matter how many promoters vouched for you.
SUID = wearing someone else's badge for one task only, then handing it back the moment the task ends.
Least privilege = giving someone the one specific key they need for their job, not a master key "just in case."
Sticky bit on /tmp = a shared fridge where everyone can put food in, but only the person who put a container in (or the building manager) can take it back out.
connections: Session 12 (Kernel): the kernel is the actual enforcement engine for every permission check — permissions are a policy, the kernel is the mechanism that makes the policy real on every syscall.

Session 13 (Processes): a process's effective permissions are inherited from the user context it runs under, which is why "what account is this actually running as" is always the first troubleshooting question.
Session 17 (Services): service accounts are a direct, practical application of least-privilege permission design — a service should run with the narrowest identity that lets it do its job.

Session 18 (Logging): permission-denied events are themselves log entries, and enterprise logging pipelines specifically capture and alert on repeated access-denied patterns as a possible attack indicator.

Session 19 (File Systems): permissions are physically stored as file system metadata (inode mode bits, NTFS security descriptors) — this session is the direct continuation of that one, adding the rules layered on top of the storage structure already covered.

Session 7 (Virtualization) and Session 8 (Boot Process): even boot-time files and hypervisor- managed virtual disks have underlying permission models controlling which processes or VMs can touch them.

This session directly sets up Users (21) and Groups (22) — the identities permissions are actually assigned to — and lays the technical foundation for the entire Layer 6 Security block, especially Least Privilege (85), Defense in Depth (86), and Zero Trust (87).
18. Diagrams (Described) Diagram A — POSIX permission string anatomy
[-][rwx][r-x][r--] → Position 1: file type. Positions 2-4: Owner rights (read, write, execute all granted).
Positions 5-7: Group rights (read and execute only, no write). Positions 8-10: Other/world rights (read only). Reading left to right always follows the fixed order: type, owner, group, other.

Diagram B — NTFS access evaluation flow [User requests access] → [Gather all SIDs: user + every group membership] → [Collect all applicable ACEs: explicit + inherited] → [Check for ANY explicit Deny matching a held SID: if found, DENY immediately] → [Check for ANY Allow matching a held SID covering the requested right: if found, ALLOW] → [If neither found, DENY by default].

Diagram C — Privilege escalation via SUID [Low-privilege user] → [Executes SUID binary owned by root] → [Process runs with root's UID for its duration] → [If the binary has a flaw (buffer overflow, unsafe input handling), attacker can hijack that root-level execution] → [Full root compromise from a low-privilege starting point]. This is why unnecessary SUID binaries are treated as active security risk, not neutral configuration.
